results.summary: Arctic0 is a 16-bit multi-cycle CPU that executes programs from an external SPI NOR flash and uses SPI SRAM for data storage. It communicates over UART for serial I/O and provides 8 GPIO inputs and 8 GPIO outputs. The design requires external SPI flash, SPI SRAM, and a USB-serial adapter for operation. It is notable for its comprehensive test suite covering ISA, memory boundaries, and FPGA bring-up.

This project implements an I2C slave that emulates a sensor with eight writable configuration registers and eight read-only registers driven by an internal LFSR. It operates at standard, fast, and fast-mode-plus speeds and is intended as a reusable template for real I2C sensors. The design was verified on an FPGA with an ESP32-C6 master, requiring only external pull-up resistors on SCL and SDA. It provides a device signature and handles unmapped addresses gracefully.

This design is a naive stream cipher demonstration that XORs an 8-bit data register with an 8-bit key register. The registers are loaded via input pins with a rising-edge trigger and a select signal. The output is the XOR result, and the bidirectional pins are inputs only. It is a proof-of-concept with minimal documentation and no silicon test results.

This project is a traffic light controller implemented as a finite state machine with five states controlling main road, side road, and pedestrian lights. It includes a pedestrian button input and outputs for eight LEDs. The design requires external LEDs with current-limiting resistors for visual indication. It is a simple educational example of an FSM.

This design is a washing machine controller implemented as a finite state machine that simulates a simplified washing process. It uses inputs for start, mode select, and door closed, and outputs for water valve, wash motor, spin motor, and a done LED. External hardware includes LEDs, a debounced button, and levers for mode and door simulation. It is a basic educational FSM project.

This project is a VGA demo titled 'Car Trip' that generates a video signal with RGB and sync outputs. The documentation is minimal, stating only that it calculates stuff and that testing instructions are not yet written. It requires a VGA PMod for display. The design's functionality is largely undocumented, so its exact behavior is unclear.

This PWM generator produces a pulse-width modulated signal with configurable period and duty cycle via 8-bit input pins. It uses an 8-bit counter and comparator, with asynchronous reset and synchronous enable. The output can drive an LED to show brightness or be measured with an oscilloscope. It is a straightforward utility block for PWM generation.

This design analyses an input PWM signal to measure its duty cycle and frequency, displaying the results on a 4-digit 7-segment display. A mode switch toggles between duty cycle and frequency display, and the frequency counter handles 1-9999 kHz with error messages for out-of-range or faulty signals. It requires an external 7-segment display and a PWM signal source. The design is useful for characterizing PWM signals in real-time.

This project implements a multiplierless shift-add tree for image convolution using binary signed-digit (BSD) arithmetic. It reads eight 8-bit values into registers and computes a weighted sum with shifts, outputting a 26-bit result in BSD format multiplexed over 8 output pins. Control signals on bidirectional pins manage register writing and output chunk selection. It is a specialized arithmetic unit for efficient convolution.

This is a three-channel RGB PWM controller that generates independent PWM signals for red, green, and blue LEDs based on stored brightness values. It includes a programmable clock divider to adjust the PWM frequency range. The design is intended to drive RGB LEDs or external driver stages, requiring current-limiting resistors for direct LED connection. It was tested using cocotb and Icarus Verilog simulation.
